rationale: PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait aortic stenosis because its concept fields align directly (trait_reported="Aortic stenosis", trait_efo="aortic stenosis") whereas PGS005255 is primarily a hemodynamic measurement score (trait_reported="Mean pressure gradient", trait_efo includes "aortic measurement"), making endpoint fidelity weaker despite both using the same phenotyping_reported (incident aortic stenosis) and identical basic covariates. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the remaining differentiators favor PGS005254: it has a stronger reported effect size (HR 1.64 vs 1.53) and a larger training sample (205,483 vs 98,645) within the same publication/method/ancestry/validation context.

PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence for the broad target trait arthritis: it reports clean PGS-only metrics (AUROC 0.539 and PGS-only R² 0.00291) with basic covariates and these are sanity-consistent with the provided low heritability ceiling context, whereas PGS004547 provides no AUROC/R² at all (only an OR=1.262, which is weak-to-moderate) and has unknown covariates. Although PGS004547 uses a more complex/meta-PRS method and many more variants, its endpoint label ('M13 Other arthritis') is narrower and its lack of comparable performance metrics makes it less well-supported than PGS001135’s directly comparable PRS-only evaluation.

PGS001135 is better supported on-record for the generic target trait “arthritis”: it has explicit PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.539 and PGS-only R²=0.00291) with basic covariates and these metrics are sanity-consistent with the provided low heritability ceiling. It also includes multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS), giving at least some transportability evidence beyond EUR. In contrast, PGS004477 is for a narrower endpoint (“M13 Other arthritis”) and provides no AUROC/R² at all (only an OR=1.20, which is weak-to-moderate), with unknown covariates and EUR-only evaluation, leaving substantially less directly comparable evidence despite its genome-wide variant count.

PGS004913 is better supported for the target because it is explicitly disease-focused on the exact endpoint (“Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis” in both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported) and reports a strong PRS stratification effect (OR top vs bottom deciles = 4.4), with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). In contrast, PGS000704 comes from a broad biomarker genetics framework paper (less endpoint-focused), provides only a full-model C-index/AUC=0.711 (not PRS-only) plus a modest HR=1.18, and includes time-to-event modeling; without PRS-only metrics its apparent discrimination is likely covariate-driven and less comparable. Both map to the same EFO and are largely EUR-evaluated, so endpoint fidelity and effect-size evidence favor PGS004913.

PGS002089 is the better match to the target trait as a straightforward ankylosing spondylitis diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both AS), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) formulation, which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic disease-risk target. Although PGS001268 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.7346/0.1023), it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 10-variant snpnet model—an archetype flagged as less reliable for external generalization. PGS002089, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (22,026) and is evaluated across multiple non-EUR groups (EUR/GME/SAS), supporting portability. Confidence is low because PGS002089’s performance evidence is limited to partial-r and lacks directly comparable PRS-only AUROC/R2, while PGS001268 provides explicit PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance metrics don’t clearly separate them. PGS000753 is from a disease-focused AAA genetic-architecture study (MVP/Mayo-VDB) with a directly stated prevalent AAA endpoint and provides a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.37), which is meaningful PRS signal evidence in the absence of AUC/R2. PGS002054 comes from a UK Biobank portability/framework paper; despite a much larger genome-wide LDpred2 score and broader evaluation ancestries, its only visible quantitative performance is a very small partial correlation (partial-r=0.0144) and it carries the framework/portability penalty. Given domain guidance favoring disease-focused endpoint-faithful models over portability-framework scores when metric evidence is weak, PGS000753 is better supported overall.

Both candidates have exact endpoint fidelity for ankylosing spondylitis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array etc.), so phenotype/covariate comparability is essentially tied. PGS001267 has clearly reported PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.7265 and PGS-only R2=0.0988) whereas PGS002089 reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its predictive evidence less directly interpretable. Although both come from UKB framework-style papers, PGS002089’s larger variant count and training N do not outweigh PGS001267’s cleaner, directly comparable PRS-only metrics; PGS001267’s PGS-only R2 is also below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability~0.399), so it passes the sanity check.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis) and have similarly light, non-clinical covariates and identical EUR evaluation size (n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. With metrics largely non-discriminating, structural/model-quality signals dominate: PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to a polygenic disease like atopic eczema than PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNPs. The reported HR separation is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (HR 1.249 vs 1.153). PGS004587’s multi-cohort training list is supportive, but not enough to outweigh the much stronger method/coverage and effect-size evidence in PGS002755.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis), but PGS001777 is better supported as a disease-focused, endpoint-specific score: it comes from a cirrhosis-focused study (“genetic risk score and diabetes predict development of alcohol-related cirrhosis in drinkers”) and shows strong PRS signal via a large effect size (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18; β=1.132). PGS000704 is a high-throughput UKB-derived snpnet model from a biomarkers genetics paper, with only modest PRS effect (HR per SD = 1.18) and a full-model C-index (0.711) that is not PRS-comparable; its larger variant count and training/validation size don’t compensate for the weaker PRS effect evidence and more framework-like study archetype. Neither reports PGS-only AUC/R2, so effect-size strength and study/endpoint focus drive the decision in favor of PGS001777.

PGS002755 is the better-supported choice for generic atopic eczema risk because its endpoint is closer to the target concept (phenotyping_reported: incident atopic dermatitis, not restricted severity) and it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with ~1.09M variants, which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic trait than PGS001773’s 25-variant GWAS-hit score for moderate-to-severe disease. PGS001773’s only strong-looking metric is AUROC=0.93/R²=0.49, but these are full-model metrics (no PGS-only AUC/R²) and are paired with covariates including parental ethnicity, making the discrimination hard to attribute to the PRS and also implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.07) as a PRS signal. PGS002755 lacks PRS-only metrics too, but provides a PRS effect size (HR high vs low PRS=1.249) in a very large European evaluation (n=337,910) with relatively standard covariates, making it the more credible standalone PRS candidate here.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is directly aligned (trait_reported: “Alcohol use disorder”, trait_efo: “alcohol dependence”, phenotyping_reported: “Alcohol use disorder”), whereas PGS000201 is framed as “Problematic alcohol use” with an EFO mapped to an alcohol dependence measurement and a DSM-5 criteria count phenotype (closer but less direct than a case/control AUD endpoint). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance comparison relies on available effect-size evidence: PGS002739 provides a clear case-control discrimination signal (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76), while PGS000201 reports only a small incremental ΔR² (0.01192) and a beta on a transformed criteria-count outcome, which is less directly interpretable for dependence risk. Although PGS000201 has cleaner disclosed covariates and a much larger genome-wide variant set, PGS002739’s stronger endpoint fidelity and more directly interpretable risk stratification evidence outweigh those advantages for this specific alcohol dependence target.

PGS002738 is the better match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is explicitly a clinical disorder construct (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo: alcohol dependence), whereas PGS000201 is centered on “Problematic alcohol use” with trait_efo mapped to an alcohol dependence measurement and a DSM-5 criteria count (log-transformed), which is a more quantitative/problem-use phenotype rather than a direct dependence diagnosis. Neither candidate reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared on PRS-comparable discrimination; however, PGS002738 provides a stronger risk-stratification effect size (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96) than the modest ΔR² reported for PGS000201 (0.01192). Although PGS000201 has cleaner/basic covariates listed, PGS002738’s disease-focused framing and closer endpoint fidelity to dependence outweigh that advantage given the lack of PRS-only metrics in both.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (M13 Other arthritis), same mapped EFO (arthritis), same training cohort (UKB), same training N (174,489), same EUR-only dev/eval ancestry, same variant count (1,059,939), same validation N (56,192), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 or covariates. With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the available effect size and any structural method advantage. PGS004547 shows a higher OR per SD (1.262) than PGS004477 (1.196), indicating stronger PRS signal, and its method (RFDiseasemetaPRS) suggests an aggregated/meta-PRS approach versus a single LDpred2 score, which is a positive structural signal when endpoints are identical. Therefore PGS004547 is better supported on the visible fields.

PGS001267 is the better match to the target trait as a generic ankylosing spondylitis diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Ankylosing spondylitis”), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) endpoint (“Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)”, phenotyping_reported “TTE ankylosing spondylitis”), which is a noted endpoint-fidelity warning for a generic disease-risk target. The two candidates are otherwise near-clones (same snpnet method, 10 variants, UKB-only training, same covariates, same ancestry distribution, same validation N), and while PGS001268 has slightly higher PRS-only AUC/R2, the metric gap is small and does not outweigh the cleaner endpoint alignment of PGS001267.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (same trait_reported/trait_efo). However, PGS003972 is supported by a large, disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis context (many contributing cohorts listed) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants, which is structurally better suited to capture polygenic signal than PGS000753’s sparse P+T score with 29 variants. Performance metrics are limited for both: PGS003972 reports only a full-model AUROC=0.69 (not PRS-comparable and covariates are unknown), while PGS000753 lacks AUC/R2 but does provide a moderate OR per SD of 1.37 with basic covariates and broader evaluation ancestry. Overall, the stronger methodological/variant-coverage and multi-cohort disease-study support for PGS003972 outweigh PGS000753’s cleaner covariate disclosure and effect-size-only evidence, but confidence is tempered because neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on structural and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far broader variant coverage (326,000 vs 858 for PGS002739’s gene-based PRS-CSx), which is a positive structural signal for a polygenic disorder when comparable PRS-only metrics are absent. Its reported discrimination proxy is also slightly stronger (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51] vs 1.76 [1.32–2.34]). PGS002739 has a clearer AFR evaluation context and includes PGC in training cohorts, but it is evaluated only in AFR and is much sparser, with no compensating PRS-only performance metrics. Overall, PGS002738 is better supported as a standalone AUD/alcohol dependence PRS.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo aortic stenosis; incident aortic stenosis phenotyping) and are EUR-trained/EUR-evaluated with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported, so we must lean on effect-size evidence, covariate comparability, and study support. PGS005254 has a much larger training sample (n=205,483 vs 47,691) and reports a well-specified PRS association with HR=1.64 including CI (1.50–1.78), under relatively basic covariates (age, age^2, sex, PCs), making the genetic signal more directly interpretable. PGS005252 reports a higher HR (1.92) but only as a point estimate and its only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index/AUC=0.87 alongside a heavy comorbidity/clinical covariate set (T2D, HTN, CAD, hyperlipidemia, BMI, smoking, renal failure), which is likely covariate-driven and not comparable to PRS performance. Given the cleaner covariate context and stronger training support, PGS005254 is better-supported overall despite the slightly lower HR point estimate.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): it has exact trait alignment (trait_reported and trait_efo both aortic stenosis) and endpoint fidelity (incident aortic stenosis cases). PGS005255 is more phenotype-adjacent/measurement-focused (trait_reported = mean pressure gradient; trait_efo includes aortic measurement), making it less directly aligned to the disease target even though its phenotyping_reported mentions incident aortic stenosis. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size and design signals: PGS005252 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.92 vs 1.53) and has a larger external validation sample (446,895 vs 244,450). Although PGS005252 reports a high full-model C-index (0.87), it uses many clinical covariates (comorbidities/BMI/smoking/renal failure) so that metric is not treated as PRS-comparable; still, the stronger HR plus cleaner disease labeling outweigh PGS005255’s simpler covariate set and larger training n.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo alcoholic liver cirrhosis), but PGS004913 has better endpoint fidelity in phenotyping_reported (explicit “Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis”) whereas PGS001777’s phenotyping_reported is “Cirrhosis (males)”, which is less specific and sex-restricted. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS001777’s AUROC=0.671 is a full-model metric and its covariates are unknown, making that discrimination hard to attribute to the PRS. PGS004913 reports an R²=0.029 and OR=4.4 (top vs bottom deciles) with clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, 10 PCs), and it has larger, multi-cohort development/validation (training n=3,037; validation n=3,360 vs 1,390). Overall, PGS004913 is better supported and more comparable for the intended disease endpoint.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all abdominal aortic aneurysm) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance is hard to compare directly. PGS003972 is better supported by study archetype and construction: it comes from a disease-focused AAA GWAS meta-analysis with many contributing cohorts/biobanks (vs PGS002054 from a UKB portability framework paper), and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with broader variant coverage (1,118,997 vs 592,187). The only quantitative metric for PGS002054 is a very small partial correlation (0.0144), while PGS003972’s reported AUROC=0.69 is full-model and not PRS-comparable, so it is not decisive but is at least consistent with a clinically oriented evaluation. Overall, the disease-focused multi-cohort provenance and larger genome-wide model make PGS003972 the stronger choice despite missing PRS-only metrics and unknown covariates.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC (0.78 in PGS005313 vs 0.74 in PGS002814) is only weakly informative. On structural and transportability signals, PGS005313 is better supported: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage cross-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with far broader variant coverage (1,271,239 vs 4,520) and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (European, African, South Asian, East Asian, Hispanic/LatAm, Other) rather than EAS-only evaluation for PGS002814. Effect-size evidence is also strong for both, but PGS005313’s OR per SD (1.82) remains clearly strong and is paired with broader evaluation context. PGS002814’s very large training N is not a reliable differentiator here, and its reported pseudo-R2/full-model metrics are not PRS-comparable and thus don’t outweigh the method/coverage and multi-ancestry evaluation advantages of PGS005313.

PGS001339 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance for the target endpoint: it reports explicit PRS-only AUROC=0.613 and PRS-only R2=0.02447 (no covariates), which is directly interpretable and also passes the heritability ceiling sanity check (h2_obs≈0.0157; R2 is small and not implausibly inflated). It also has clear phenotype alignment to the target via “TTE atrial fibrillation and flutter,” with basic covariates only. In contrast, PGS002050 has similar trait/phenotype wording but provides no PRS-only AUROC/R2 (only partial correlation 0.1034), making its predictive strength less directly comparable despite higher variant count and larger training N; both are UKB framework-style scores, so the decisive advantage is PGS001339’s cleaner, explicit PRS-only metrics.

PGS001263 is the better-supported match for the target trait (atrial flutter) because its endpoint is directly atrial flutter across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS001339 explicitly bundles atrial fibrillation + flutter and uses a time-to-event phenotype (TTE), reducing endpoint fidelity for a generic atrial flutter target. Both are from the same pan-trait UKB sparse snpnet framework with identical training size (n=269,704), similar covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), and the same validation size (n=24,905), so study-design signals don’t differentiate them. On PRS-comparable metrics, PGS001263 is slightly stronger (PGS-only AUROC 0.617 vs 0.613; PGS-only R2 0.02517 vs 0.02447), with both well below the heritability ceiling, making the small performance edge consistent and supportive. Given near-clone context, the direct phenotype match plus marginally better PRS-only metrics favors PGS001263.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model AUROC). With endpoint fidelity and study context indistinguishable, the only visible differentiator is slightly stronger performance signals for PGS000454: marginally higher Nagelkerke pseudo-R² (0.0489 vs 0.0487) and higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.79 vs 3.61) while AUROC is identical (0.632). Differences are small, so confidence is low, but PGS000454 has the edge on the available metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study context (same UKB portability paper), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training size, and identical reported partial-r (~0.0716) with the same multi-ancestry evaluation distribution. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes to separate them, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002032 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (19,768) versus PGS001824’s extremely sparse penalized regression score (22 variants), which is less likely to capture polygenic signal for this complex disease label. Given otherwise identical evidence, PGS002032 is better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (basal cell carcinoma), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (11,734), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation N (11,322). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so only full-model metrics/effect sizes can weakly differentiate. PGS000454 has marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.632 vs 0.630) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0489 vs 0.0456), while PGS000456 has slightly higher top-1% OR (3.95 vs 3.79). Given the essentially identical design and tiny metric differences, I pick PGS000454 on the slightly stronger overall discrimination/R² signal, but confidence is low because differences are within noise and metrics are full-model rather than PRS-only.

PGS000327 is the better-supported ASD PRS because its endpoint fidelity is clean (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all explicitly “Autism spectrum disorder”), and it comes from a disease-focused ASD GWAS meta-analysis context with clear training/validation description (multi-cohort list, training n=28,592; validation n=7,148). It also provides supportive PRS signal via an OR=1.33 per SD and an R²-type metric (0.0245) that is plausibly within the ASD heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS002790 has an explicit phenotype mismatch in the key endpoint field (phenotyping_reported = “Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)”), unclear training sample size (“N/A”), and only a small partial R² (~0.0055) from a cross-psychiatric/cognition framing, making it less directly supported as an ASD diagnosis PRS despite its larger variant count.

PGS001263 is the better-supported choice for the target trait atrial flutter because it has exact endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all = atrial flutter) and reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R2=0.025), with basic covariates only; its PGS-only R2 is also plausible relative to the provided heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.016; not an obvious misuse given scale differences). In contrast, PGS002050 uses a broader combined endpoint (atrial fibrillation and flutter) and, while it has a larger variant set and training N, it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 and provides only a partial correlation metric, making its PRS discrimination evidence less directly comparable for atrial flutter specifically.

PGS004587 is the better-supported match to the target trait (atopic eczema) because its endpoint is a generic incident atopic dermatitis diagnosis (phenotyping_reported: "Incident atopic dermatitis"), aligning well with the broad target concept, whereas PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype ("Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis"), which is a partial endpoint mismatch for a generic atopic eczema target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R²; PGS001773’s very high AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49 are full-model metrics (not PRS-comparable) and are further made less comparable by inclusion of parental ethnicity covariates, so they cannot be used as strong evidence of standalone PRS quality and the R² is implausibly above the eczema heritability ceiling. PGS004587, while also sparse (23 SNPs) and lacking AUC/R², provides a direct PRS effect estimate (HR high vs low PRS=1.153) in a very large European evaluation (n=337,910) with relatively standard covariates, making its evidence package more coherent and less likely to be dominated by covariate-driven discrimination than PGS001773.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to atrial fibrillation (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/C-index is not a clean differentiator—especially since PGS005168’s very high C-index (0.8718) is paired with explicit CHARGE-AF risk-calculator covariate packaging, making the discrimination largely non-comparable to standalone PRS performance. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that strong leakage/packaging signal, and it also shows strong PRS effect size evidence (OR 1.82 with tight CI) plus a cross-ancestry PRS-CSx construction with substantially larger variant count (1,271,239 vs 382,963), which is a positive structural signal when PRS-only metrics are absent. Overall, PGS005313 is better-supported as a cleaner PRS model for AF, while PGS005168’s performance evidence is heavily confounded by CHARGE-AF inclusion.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002788 targets the narrower subtype bipolar II disorder (type 2). Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have similar variant counts, identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, identical basic covariates (age, PCs1-3), and the same validation sample size (n=2,524), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only small partial R² full-model values). Although PGS002788 has a slightly higher partial R² (0.00307 vs 0.00251), the phenotyping_reported fields indicate these are associations with non-disease endpoints (sluggish cognitive tempo vs pattern comparison cognition), making the tiny metric difference weak and not sufficient to outweigh endpoint fidelity to the requested bipolar disorder label.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002787 is specifically bipolar I disorder (a subtype). Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), have similar variant counts and EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only small partial R² values that are not clearly PRS-only). PGS002787 has a slightly higher reported partial R² (0.00275 vs 0.00251), but given the endpoint-fidelity mismatch in phenotyping_reported for both (neither is a direct bipolar diagnosis endpoint) and the tiny metric difference, the exact trait alignment of PGS002786 is the most defensible tie-break.

PGS001824 is the cleaner phenotype match to the target (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are directly “Disorders of bilirubin excretion” mapped to bilirubin metabolism disease), whereas PGS000924 uses a broader combined endpoint (“disorders of porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism”) and is explicitly time-to-event, which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease target. Although PGS000924 reports strong-looking PRS-only AUROC/R², its PGS-only R²=0.218 exceeds the provided heritability ceiling estimate (~0.089), making the metric suspect/non-comparable on its face; PGS001824’s partial correlation is modest but does not violate the heritability sanity check. Both are UKB framework-style scores with basic covariates, so the decision hinges mainly on endpoint fidelity and metric plausibility, favoring PGS001824.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (basal cell carcinoma), same publication and release date, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sample sizes, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). With endpoints and design essentially identical, the only differentiators are small, likely-noise differences in full-model AUROC/Nagelkerke R² (PGS000452 slightly higher: 0.632 vs 0.630; 0.0487 vs 0.0456) versus top-1% OR (PGS000456 slightly higher: 3.95 vs 3.61). Given the guidance that small full-model AUC differences are weak but still the most directly comparable signal available here, PGS000452 edges out PGS000456 by marginally better overall discrimination/R²; confidence is low because the records are effectively tied and lack PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUCs are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. PGS005168 is heavily risk-packaged via inclusion of the named clinical risk calculator CHARGE-AF in covariates, making its high full-model C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and weak evidence about standalone PRS quality. In contrast, PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that packaging/leakage concern, and still shows strong PRS signal via effect size (OR≈1.94 per SD). Although PGS005168 has a stronger method family (PRS-CS) and far more variants, the explicit CHARGE-AF augmentation undermines interpretability enough that the cleaner, more comparable evaluation setup of PGS002814 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS002032 is the better-supported match to the target because its endpoint is a direct, single-concept phenotype (“Disorders of bilirubin excretion”) mapped solely to the target EFO (bilirubin metabolism disease) and it is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), which is supportive for transportability. PGS000924, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC/R²), is a pan-trait UKB framework score (“across 813 traits”) with a time-to-event composite phenotype that also includes porphyrin metabolism disease, reducing endpoint fidelity to the specific target. Given both are UKB-derived framework-style records and PGS002032 lacks PRS-only AUC/R², confidence is low, but the phenotype alignment advantage favors PGS002032.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same publication, same method (SDPR), similar genome-wide variant counts (~935k), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same basic covariates (age, PCs1-3), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only small full-model partial R² values). Endpoint fidelity to the target trait “bipolar disorder” is slightly better for PGS002787 because it targets bipolar I disorder (Type 1), which is closer to the generic bipolar disorder concept than the bipolar II (Type 2) focus of PGS002788; the phenotyping_reported fields look behavior/proxy-like for both and don’t clearly favor either. PGS002788 has a trivially higher partial R² and slightly larger validation N, but these are weak tie-breakers and the metric difference is negligible, so the broader/closer subtype match drives the choice.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Breast cancer/breast carcinoma), study context (same publication, UKB training, same training n=12,483), ancestry distribution (EUR GWAS/DEV; EVAL EUR+SAS), covariates (0), and validation size (n=48,968). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must fall back to within-family empirical signals. Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Breast cancer/breast carcinoma), study context (same publication), covariates (0), training cohort (UKB), training N (12,483), evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS), and validation N (48,968), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R², which are not ideal for PRS comparison). With endpoints and design effectively identical, the best differentiator is the within-family empirical performance: PGS004153 shows slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6625 vs 0.6598) and R² (0.0764 vs 0.0739) and slightly stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 1.826 vs 1.809; β 0.602 vs 0.593) than PGS004040. Given the small gaps and overlapping CIs, confidence is moderate rather than high, but PGS004153 has the consistent edge across the available metrics.

PGS003428 is better supported as a standalone cervical carcinoma PRS: it is disease-focused (GWAS meta-analyses of cervical phenotypes) with an explicit incident cervical cancer endpoint and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred) with very large variant coverage (2,894,555), which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic cancer risk score than a 15-SNP genome-wide-significant loci score. While neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model C-index), PGS003428 shows stronger discrimination/effect evidence (C-index 0.613; HR per SD 1.33) than PGS005165 (C-index 0.566; HR 1.2). PGS005165 also comes from a pan-cancer risk prediction framework and is a sparse known-loci score with no training sample reported, making its PRS evidence package weaker despite being in an East Asian cohort.

Both candidates align well to the target (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; trait_reported cervical cancer) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index/AUROC is only weakly informative. PGS000073 has slightly clearer endpoint fidelity via an explicit incident cervical cancer phenotype and provides richer performance reporting (AUROC 0.745 plus C-index 0.75 with SE) and similar moderate HR per SD (1.22) compared with PGS005165 (C-index 0.566; HR 1.2). While PGS005165 has more variants (15 vs 10), its substantially lower reported discrimination and narrower single-record evidence make it less supported on the visible fields. Ancestry differs (EUR vs EAS) but with no deployment ancestry specified, this does not outweigh the stronger validation/performance package for PGS000073.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation sample size (n=19,908), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r). The main differentiators are structural: PGS002072 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (428,587 vs 2,059 for PGS001861) and also has slightly higher partial correlation (0.098 vs 0.0948). Given identical context otherwise, the genome-wide LDpred2 score with higher partial-r is better supported than the sparse penalized-regression sibling here.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo cervical carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident cervical cancer; EUR evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC/C-index in PGS000073 (AUROC ~0.745) is heavily discounted—especially because it uses a much heavier covariate set (parity, oral contraceptive use, pack-years, PCs/array), making the metric less comparable to standalone PRS performance. PGS003428 comes from a cervical-phenotype GWAS meta-analysis/risk-stratification study and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred with ~2.9M variants) with cleaner covariates (age, smoking) and a slightly stronger per-SD effect size (HR 1.33 vs 1.22), which is more indicative of PRS signal when PRS-only metrics are absent. Overall evidence package favors the disease-focused, genome-wide PRS (PGS003428) over the sparse 10-variant cross-cancer score (PGS000073).

PGS001174 is a cleaner match to the target trait cholelithiasis: trait_efo is exactly cholelithiasis and phenotyping_reported is a direct cholelithiasis endpoint (albeit time-to-event), whereas PGS001861 uses a broader composite phenotype (“Cholelithiasis and cholecystitis”) with mixed trait_efo. PGS001174 also provides PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.623 and PGS-only R2=0.028), which are interpretable and pass the heritability ceiling sanity check (h2_obs≈0.021; same scale order), while PGS001861 reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.0948) and no PRS-only AUC/R2, making cross-model PRS performance comparison weaker. Although both are UKB framework-style scores with similar basic covariates and multi-ancestry evaluation, PGS001174 has stronger endpoint fidelity and more directly comparable PRS-only metrics than PGS001861.

PGS001174 is the better-supported choice for the target trait cholelithiasis because it has a direct endpoint match (trait_efo=cholelithiasis; phenotyping_reported=TTE cholelithiasis) and, critically, reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.623 and PGS-only R²=0.028) with only basic covariates; its PGS-only R² is also plausible relative to the provided h2_obs ceiling (~0.021–0.029). In contrast, PGS002072 uses a broader composite phenotype (cholelithiasis and cholecystitis; trait_efo includes cholecystitis) and does not provide PRS-only AUROC/R² (only partial correlation), making its predictive performance less directly comparable despite larger training N and a genome-wide method/variant count. Both are UKB framework-style scores with multi-ancestry evaluation, so the decisive advantage is PGS001174’s tighter phenotype alignment and clearer PRS-only metric evidence.

PGS001301 has cleaner, PRS-comparable performance reporting for celiac disease: it provides explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.82867) and PGS-only R² (0.14224) with basic covariates listed, enabling direct assessment of the genetic score contribution. Its PGS-only R² is also below the provided liability-scale heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.2305), so it passes the sanity check. In contrast, PGS000316 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.879) with covariates marked unknown and no PGS-only AUROC/R², making its apparent discrimination non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS000316 is more directly ‘Coeliac disease’ while PGS001301’s ‘Malabsorption/coeliac disease’ is slightly broader; however, the stronger PRS-only metric evidence and transparent covariate context in PGS001301 outweigh that minor phenotype-label penalty.

PGS000040 is a disease-focused celiac/coeliac disease model with direct endpoint fidelity (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both “Coeliac disease”), whereas PGS001301 comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework (“across 813 traits”) and uses a broader/less specific phenotype label (“Malabsorption/coeliac disease”), which is a mild endpoint dilution. Although PGS001301 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.8287; PGS-only R2 0.1422) and larger training/validation, it also shows a very large incremental AUROC (0.2578) relative to the small celiac h2_obs ceiling provided (0.0053), raising comparability/sanity concerns about metric scale/definition. PGS000040 lacks PRS-only metrics (only full-model AUROC 0.90, covariates unknown), but its endpoint specificity and non-framework study archetype make it the better-supported choice overall given the framework penalty and phenotype dilution on PGS001301.

PGS002237 is better supported for the target CKD endpoint: its phenotyping is a clear clinical definition (eGFR <45; stage 3+), and it shows stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR 1.47 per SD) plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/ASN/EUR/MAE), consistent with a disease-focused cross-ancestry CKD paper. PGS004158 has a broader/less specific phenotype (“CKD or dialysis”), comes from a methods-benchmarking/ensemble context with much smaller training (n=13,496), and its reported AUROC/R² are full-model metrics (no PRS-only) with modest discrimination (AUROC ~0.59; R² ~0.02) that are not clearly comparable to a standalone PRS. Overall, PGS002237 has better endpoint fidelity and more convincing disease-focused evidence despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R².

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate coeliac/celiac disease) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown), so performance is not cleanly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Given that, structural/study signals dominate: PGS000040 uses a higher-capacity statistical learning approach (SparSNP) with substantially more variants (228 vs 53) and reports a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.90 vs 0.879), while keeping the same EUR-only evaluation context. PGS000316’s main advantage is much larger validation sample size and broader listed cohorts, but validation size is a weak tie-break and its reported AUROC is still full-model. Overall, PGS000040 has the clearer model-structure advantage with no endpoint penalty, so it is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates map cleanly to COPD (same trait_efo), but PGS004536 has stronger disease-endpoint fidelity via an explicit ICD10 code phenotype (J44) and shows a strong PRS effect size (OR=1.49 per SD), which is meaningful discrimination evidence even without AUC/R2. PGS001332 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.540/0.00235, below the COPD h2 ceiling) and uses only basic covariates, but it comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“813 traits”) with a very small SNP set (482) and weak PRS-only performance, which domain guidance flags as less reliable externally than a disease-focused score. Given the framework penalty plus weak PRS-only metrics for PGS001332, PGS004536 is better-supported overall despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS001783 is better supported for generic COPD risk because it has clean PRS-comparable performance reported (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2=0.0381), which is interpretable and also plausible relative to the COPD heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0388). It also uses only basic covariates (sex, age, PCs) and is developed across many biobanks (global biobank framework), reducing reliance on a single-cohort setting. In contrast, PGS004536 targets an ICD-10 subtype label (J44) and appears to be a risk-factor–integrated metaPRS (“Integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”), which raises packaging/leakage concerns, yet it provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and has unknown covariates; the only metric shown is an OR=1.49 without clarity on adjustment. Overall, PGS001783 has clearer endpoint labeling for COPD and substantially cleaner, directly comparable PRS-only performance evidence than PGS004536.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver”) and both use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), so phenotype fidelity and leakage risk are essentially tied. PGS004621 is better supported structurally and empirically as a polygenic model: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and reports a per-SD effect size OR=1.42 plus an AUROC=0.68 (not PRS-only, but at least with basic covariates). In contrast, PGS000726 is a very sparse 12-variant GWS-hits score with no AUC/R2 reported; its main evidence is an extreme-quantile OR (top 20% vs bottom 20% = 2.26), which is less directly comparable than per-SD discrimination and doesn’t offset the limited polygenic coverage. Given similar endpoint alignment, the stronger method/coverage and more directly interpretable effect-size evidence favor PGS004621.

Both candidates match the target trait well at the concept level (trait_efo=chronic kidney disease; stage 3+ wording is essentially aligned). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the very high full-model AUROC values (0.78 in PGS002237; 0.90 in PGS005090) are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. Given that, PGS005090 is better-supported structurally and contextually for CKD risk in the evaluated population: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with substantially more variants (1,142,436 vs 471,316) and is trained/evaluated entirely in AFR/African American cohorts (MVP/REGARDS; eval n=67,819), whereas PGS002237 is developed in EUR-only (UKB) with a smaller validation (n=11,813) and includes a heavier clinical covariate bundle (including hypertension/diabetes, medication use), making its reported full-model AUROC less interpretable for PRS contribution. Effect sizes are similar (OR 1.41 vs 1.47), so the method/ancestry-aligned evaluation package favors PGS005090.

PGS005090 is better supported for the target trait CKD because its endpoint is more specific and clinically anchored ("Chronic kidney disease (stage 3 or higher)" with phenotyping_reported "Chronic kidney disease") and it comes from a CKD-in-Black-American-populations focused study with AFR-only development/evaluation, matching a clear transportability context. Although its reported AUROC=0.9 is only a full-model metric and likely covariate-influenced (age/sex/diabetes/PCs) with no PRS-only AUC/R2, it at least provides a moderate PRS effect size (OR 1.41). In contrast, PGS004158 is from a multi-biobank methods evaluation/ensemble framework with a broader/less clean phenotype definition ("Chronic kidney disease or dialysis"), and its reported AUROC (~0.59) is also full-model with no PRS-only metrics; additionally, its covariates field is "0" (unclear modeling context) and its development is EUR-only with mixed EUR/SAS evaluation, making it less directly aligned to a coherent CKD endpoint package than PGS005090.

PGS004621 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are directly “Cirrhosis/cirrhosis of liver,” whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to “Alcoholic cirrhosis” (alcoholic liver cirrhosis), a subtype mismatch for a generic cirrhosis target. Study archetype/transportability also favors PGS004621: it comes from a disease-focused cirrhosis genetics paper with multi-cohort development (AllofUs, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) and very large European evaluation (n=1,153,995), versus PGS000704 from a broader UKB biomarker framework with single-cohort development (UKB) and mixed EUR/MAE evaluation. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index/AUROC (0.711 for PGS000704 vs 0.68 for PGS004621) is not decisive; instead, PGS004621’s stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.42 vs HR 1.18) plus cleaner endpoint alignment and broader multi-cohort context outweigh PGS000704’s slightly higher full-model metric.

Both candidates align to the target COPD at the trait_reported/trait_efo level, but PGS001783 has cleaner endpoint wording (phenotyping_reported exactly COPD) than PGS001332 (“Chronic obstructive airways disease/copd,” slightly broader). On PRS-comparable performance, PGS001783 reports a substantially higher PRS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.0381 versus PGS001332 PGS R2 (no covariates)=0.00235 and PGS-only AUROC=0.5397; PGS001783’s R2 also matches the provided COPD heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0388) as a plausible upper-bound sanity check. Study archetype/method also favors PGS001783: PRS-CS-auto with ~884k variants from a global multi-biobank analysis (many cohorts, multi-ancestry GWAS) is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than PGS001332’s very sparse snpnet (482 variants) from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” framework, which is a negative generalizability signal despite its larger validation N and multi-ancestry eval mix. Overall, PGS001783 is better-supported on endpoint fidelity + PRS signal strength + study/method context.

ontology: congenital vitamin k-dependent coagulation factors deficiency
rationale: Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), and validation size (n=19,864). The partial-r being the same suggests no empirical advantage for the sparse model (PGS001826), so the better-supported choice is PGS002034.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait/phenotyping (breast cancer; EFO breast carcinoma), same publication, same variant count (1,041,298), same ancestry distribution and cohorts (UKB; EUR GWAS/DEV; EUR+SAS eval), same training (n=12,483) and validation size (n=48,968), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics shown). Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all corneal dystrophy), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation size (n=19,321).
