PGS001835 is an extremely sparse penalized-regression score with weaker partial-r, offering less evidence of capturing polygenic signal here. Hence PGS002042 is better supported.

PGS000726 is the better-supported match to the target trait (cirrhosis of liver): its trait_efo is exactly "cirrhosis of liver" and phenotyping_reported is the generic diagnosis "Cirrhosis", whereas PGS000704 is explicitly restricted to the subtype "Alcoholic cirrhosis" (trait_efo "alcoholic liver cirrhosis"), which is a narrower endpoint and a partial mismatch for a generic cirrhosis target. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS000704’s reported C-index 0.711 is a full-model metric and not a clean PRS-comparable advantage; by contrast PGS000726 provides supportive PRS signal via effect sizes (OR per SD 1.32; OR top vs bottom quintile 2.26) and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort cirrhosis genetics study with broader cohort base and multi-ancestry evaluation, while PGS000704 is UKB-only development from a broad biomarker genetics framework with endpoint less central to the paper. Overall, endpoint fidelity and study archetype favor PGS000726.

Both candidates match the target CAD endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all coronary artery disease) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS000013 also chip), so phenotype fidelity and leakage risk are similar. PGS003725 is better supported as a disease-focused, explicitly multi-ancestry CAD PRS with broad evaluation across AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/MAE/SAS and strong per-SD effect sizes (HR 1.75; OR 2.14), indicating substantial PRS signal even without AUC/R2. PGS000013 does report a PRS-comparable R2=0.04 (below the CAD h2_liability ceiling, so plausible), but its headline AUROC=0.81 is full-model and not PRS-only, and it lacks similarly strong effect-size evidence on the visible record. Given the stronger discriminative effect-size evidence plus broader multi-ancestry evaluation context, PGS003725 edges out PGS000013 despite missing PRS-only R2/AUC.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all coronary artery disease) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on study archetype/transportability and effect-size evidence. PGS003725 comes from a CAD-focused multi-ancestry PRS paper (Nat Med) with explicitly broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/MAE/SAS) and shows stronger reported per-SD discrimination (OR 2.14 and HR 1.75) than PGS002244 (OR 1.64 only). Covariates are similarly light (age/sex/PCs) in both. Although PGS002244 has more variants and slightly larger training/validation Ns, it is from a pan-disease ‘across ancestries in one million people’ framework-style publication and lacks the stronger effect-size support seen in PGS003725. Overall, PGS003725 is better supported for CAD risk prediction on the visible fields.

PGS005170 is the better-supported match to the target trait dementia: it directly targets all-cause dementia with incident all-cause dementia phenotyping, uses a much stronger structural approach (integrative ensemble of 24 component PRSs with genome-wide methods; 1,320,229 variants) and shows multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR), whereas PGS000823 is a sparse 23-variant GWAS-hits score labeled Alzheimer’s disease with only EUR evaluation. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS005170’s full-model AUROC=0.761 cannot be treated as PRS performance, but its per-SD HR=1.25 plus richer method/coverage and broader transportability evidence outweigh PGS000823’s only reported contrast HR (top vs bottom tertile)=1.36 and minimal covariate set. Confidence is moderate because both lack clean PRS-only metrics and PGS005170 includes APOE genotype covariates, making the AUROC less PRS-comparable.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/all-cause dementia; trait_efo=dementia), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS004281 (0.819 vs 0.761) is not a reliable differentiator. PGS005170 is better-supported structurally and for transportability: it is an integrative ensemble of 24 component PRSs with genome-wide scale (1,320,229 variants) and shows multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR), plus it reports an HR per SD (1.25, 95% CI 1.11–1.42) as direct PRS signal. PGS004281 is a very sparse 110-variant single-UKB score evaluated only in EUR; its apparent AUROC advantage is full-model and could be largely covariate-driven. Overall, PGS005170 has the stronger disease-focused, externally oriented evidence package despite smaller listed training n.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all coronary artery disease) and use similar basic covariates without obvious clinical-risk packaging. PGS000013’s main advantage is reporting a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2=0.04), but its headline AUROC=0.81 is a full-model metric and not directly comparable as PRS performance. PGS002244, despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, has stronger supportive evidence via a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.64 with tight CI) and a larger training/validation scale (175,364 train; 343,676 validation vs 120,280; 288,978) with clearly multi-ancestry evaluation. Given domain guidance that strong OR/HR can outweigh modest PRS-only R2 from an older portability-style score, PGS002244 is better-supported overall, though confidence is tempered by its missing PRS-comparable metrics.

PGS004281 is the better match to the target trait dementia on endpoint fidelity: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “All-cause dementia” with trait_efo=dementia, whereas PGS000823 is primarily an Alzheimer’s disease score (trait_reported AD; trait_efo Alzheimer disease) despite having phenotyping_reported “Incident all-cause dementia,” creating a concept mismatch for a generic dementia target. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS004281’s full-model AUROC (0.819) cannot be treated as PRS-comparable, but it is at least a coherent reported discrimination signal under basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) and a large EUR evaluation (n=67,428). PGS000823 offers only a modest HR (1.36 top vs bottom tertile) with smaller evaluation (n=12,978) and lacks training sample information, so overall support is weaker for dementia as the target endpoint.

PGS000997 is better supported for the target trait (diverticular disease) because it has tighter endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported is explicitly “TTE diverticular disease of intestine” mapping cleanly to diverticular disease) whereas PGS000996 mixes endpoints (“diverticular disease/diverticulitis” and trait_efo includes diverticulitis). Both are from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework with identical training cohort, covariates, and ancestry setup, so performance becomes the key differentiator: PGS000997 shows materially stronger PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.591 vs 0.552; PGS-only R² 0.0178 vs 0.0037) and higher incremental AUROC (0.0173 vs 0.0084). Variant count also favors PGS000997 (5757 vs 368) within the same method/publication family. Both PRS-only R² values are within the provided heritability ceiling sanity range, so the higher PRS-only signal in PGS000997 is credible.

Both candidates target the same trait and are MTAG DCM PRS-CS scores evaluated in Europeans, so endpoint fidelity is broadly comparable; PGS004951 is slightly more clinically explicit (“Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy”) than PGS004862 (“Dilated cardiomyopathy”). The key differentiator is performance evidence isolating PRS contribution: PGS004951 reports an explicit univariate (PRS-only) AUC=0.67 (with CI) and delta R² metrics (liability-scale delta 0.101), whereas PGS004862 reports only full-model AUROC=0.71/R²=0.05 with covariates (age/sex/PCs) and no PRS-only/incremental metrics, making its AUROC less comparable as a PRS measure. PGS004951 also shows a stronger per-SD OR (1.93 vs 1.76) and higher variant count (1,075,760 vs 709,534); its multi-ancestry GWAS (EUR+MAE) is not penalized given EUR-only evaluation. Validation N is much larger for PGS004862, but per guidance this is a weak tie-break and doesn’t outweigh the cleaner PRS-only metric evidence and stronger effect size in PGS004951.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet paper, same method (PRS-CS), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same phenotyping_reported (Dilated cardiomyopathy), same covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), and same validation sample size (n=347,585), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). Given this tie on endpoint fidelity and study context, PGS004862 is preferred because it is the MTAG-enhanced version (trait_reported: "Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)") which domain guidance explicitly mildly prefers over the base DCM score, and it also shows slightly stronger reported signals in the selected record (AUROC 0.71 vs 0.70; R² 0.05 vs 0.048; OR 1.76 vs 1.56). Confidence is Moderate because the performance differences are small and are full-model rather than PRS-only metrics.

PGS004951 is better supported for dilated cardiomyopathy because it provides PRS-comparable performance evidence (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.67 with CI and delta PRS/residual liability-scale R²=0.101), whereas PGS004861 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.70/0.048) without isolating PRS contribution. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (both map to dilated cardiomyopathy; PGS004951’s phenotyping is explicitly clinical DCM and MTAG is not a negative per the provided policy). Although PGS004861 has a much larger validation sample (n=347,585) and slightly cleaner/basic covariates, validation size is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh PGS004951’s clearer PRS-only metrics plus stronger effect size (OR 1.93 vs 1.56) and larger genome-wide variant set (1,075,760 vs 713,932) within the same method family (PRS-CS).

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and consistent phenotyping_reported). However, PGS001254 comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 11-variant snpnet model—an archetype flagged as less reliable for external generalization despite having clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; R² 0.0247) in EUR. PGS002092, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R², is a genome-wide LDpred2 score with very large variant coverage (484,484) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger transportability evidence than the EUR-only evaluation of PGS001254. Given the framework-penalty and sparsity concerns for PGS001254, the broader-coverage, multi-ancestry-evaluated PGS002092 is better-supported overall.

PGS004614 is the better-supported diverticular disease PRS on endpoint fidelity and study archetype: it targets exactly “Diverticular disease” across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported and comes from a disease-focused publication, with genome-wide shrinkage (SBayesR) and very large variant coverage (1,082,282) plus explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/SAS). PGS000996, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.5519; R2 0.00372, below the heritability ceiling) and has large UKB training, is from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a combined diverticular disease/diverticulitis endpoint and a very sparse model (368 variants), which domain guidance flags as typically less reliable externally. PGS004614’s reported AUROC (0.76) is full-model and includes family history (covariate leakage concern), so confidence is not high, but overall the disease-focused, endpoint-faithful, genome-wide model outweighs the framework score’s modest PRS-only performance.

PGS000997 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence for diverticular disease: it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.591 and PGS-only R2=0.0178) with basic covariates and a large, clearly specified UKB training set plus multi-ancestry evaluation. In contrast, PGS004614 only provides a full-model AUROC (0.76) while using family history as a covariate and gives no PRS-only AUC/R2, making its apparent performance largely non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven; its training sample size is also not reported. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (both map to diverticular disease), so the decisive difference is the availability and cleanliness of PRS-only performance evidence favoring PGS000997 despite its framework-paper origin.

Both candidates align well to the target endpoint (trait_efo = Dupuytren Contracture; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/contracture diagnosis). However, PGS001254 comes from the pan-trait UKB sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 11-variant model, which is a known warning archetype for weaker external generalization despite having clean PRS-only AUROC/R² reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; R² 0.0247) and EUR-only evaluation. PGS001880, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R², is a genome-wide penalized regression score with far broader variant coverage (2443 variants) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), providing stronger transportability evidence for real-world use. Given the framework+sparsity risk in PGS001254 versus the broader, multi-ancestry-evaluated construction in PGS001880, PGS001880 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates are essentially matched on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported for Dupuytren’s disease), study archetype (same UKB portability paper), training size (n=391,124), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation sample size (n=18,971), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiators are structural: PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (484,484 vs 2,443 for PGS001880’s penalized regression sparse score), and it has a slightly higher partial correlation (0.0797 vs 0.0783). With metrics otherwise near-tied, the broader genome-wide model plus marginally better partial-r supports PGS002092.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_efo=follicular lymphoma; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported=Nodular lymphoma), from the same publication, with identical EUR-only ancestry context, training size (n=3,696), validation size (n=3,256), and the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference is only weakly informative; still, PGS000644 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.538 vs 0.532) and slightly higher Nagelkerke R² (0.00349 vs 0.00282) and per-SD OR (1.149 vs 1.133). PGS000643’s higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.49 vs 1.48) is a counter-signal, making this a close call, but overall the broader/average performance indicators marginally favor PGS000644.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis, same phenotyping_reported/trait_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis, same method PRSCS, same evaluation ancestry mix and validation n=94,651) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative. Given otherwise matched endpoint fidelity and study context, PGS005271 has consistently stronger available performance signals than PGS005272 (higher full-model AUROC 0.6297 vs 0.6054 and stronger effect sizes OR per SD 1.55 vs 1.42; beta 0.438 vs 0.349), making it the better-supported choice on the visible fields.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). PGS001789 has a clear PRS-comparable metric reported (pgs_only_r2 / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 = 0.0312), whereas PGS004160 reports only full-model AUROC/R² (0.694 / 0.089) with no PGS-only AUC/R², making its performance less directly interpretable as standalone PRS. PGS001789 is also developed in a broad multi-biobank context with multi-ancestry GWAS inputs and large evaluation (n=359,345) versus PGS004160’s single-UKB development (samples_training n=6,704) and smaller evaluation (n=90,274). Although PGS004160 has an ensemble-style method label and reports strong OR per SD (~2.05), the lack of PRS-only metrics and narrower development context leave it less well-supported on the visible fields than PGS001789.

PGS002304 is the cleaner endpoint match to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” whereas PGS000643 is labeled “Nodular lymphoma” (despite mapping to follicular lymphoma in trait_efo), introducing phenotype/label ambiguity. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not strong cross-model PRS evidence; however, PGS002304’s higher reported AUROC (0.61 vs 0.532) comes without any explicit covariate packaging, while PGS000643’s evaluation is explicitly adjusted for age/sex/batch/PCs, making its full-model metric more clearly covariate-influenced and less comparable to standalone PRS performance. Although PGS000643 has a stronger genome-wide method (PRS-CS) and many more variants plus larger validation n, endpoint fidelity is the primary criterion here and favors PGS002304.

PGS002304 is the better-supported match for the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is exact: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both “Follicular lymphoma,” aligning cleanly with the target, whereas PGS000644 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” despite mapping to the same EFO, introducing avoidable phenotype ambiguity. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are not cleanly comparable PRS metrics; however, even on those reported full-model AUROCs PGS002304 is higher (0.61 vs 0.538). PGS000644 has stronger structural properties (lassosum, ~2.2M variants) and clearer basic covariates, but it comes from a PRSweb repository-style framework context and its performance evidence remains modest; given the domain emphasis on phenotype alignment as the top factor when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS002304 wins.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported/trait_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication, and have identical evaluation ancestry and validation sample size (n=94,651), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported in either (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS metric). With endpoint and validation context essentially tied, the differentiators are structural and effect-size evidence: PGS005272 uses PRS-CS with genome-wide coverage (1,085,142 variants) and shows a much stronger per-SD effect size (OR≈1.42) than PGS005270 (OR≈1.04), which is consistent with materially better PRS discriminative signal. The slightly higher full-model AUROC for PGS005270 (0.639 vs 0.605) is discounted as non-PRS-only and small enough to be unreliable for ranking here.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), study context (same publication, UKB training n=6,704), covariates (both 0), ancestry distribution (DEV EUR; EVAL EUR+SAS), and validation size (n=90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC/R²). Given that, small full-model AUROC differences are weak but still within-family informative: PGS004160 shows consistently higher full-model AUROC (0.694 vs 0.685), higher R² (0.089 vs 0.080), and slightly stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 2.05 vs 2.00; β 0.717 vs 0.693) than PGS004047. It also has a higher variant count (976,174 vs 865,644) and is an ensemble/multi-PRS method, which is a positive structural signal when other fields are essentially identical.

PGS002728 is better supported on endpoint fidelity and study archetype: it targets hip osteoarthritis with phenotyping_reported as total hip replacement (a clinically specific, hip-OA–proximal endpoint) and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort context (multiple development cohorts listed) with basic covariates (age, sex). PGS004478 matches the EFO but is an ICD-code style label (M16 coxarthrosis) from a risk-factor integration paper with unknown covariates and provides only a single OR (1.296 per SD; moderate) with no PRS-comparable AUC/R2. Since neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, the cleaner endpoint/covariate transparency and disease-focused multi-cohort support in PGS002728 outweigh PGS004478’s genome-wide method/variant count advantage.

PGS002763 is the better-supported match to the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is direct and clean: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Hip osteoarthritis,” aligning tightly with the target. PGS004478 maps to the same EFO term but is presented as an ICD-style code label (“M16 (Coxarthrosis [arthrosis of hip])”), which is likely equivalent but slightly less transparent as an endpoint description. Neither candidate reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so performance can’t be separated on clean metrics; however, PGS002763 shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.38 with CI 1.31–1.46) than PGS004478 (OR ~1.296 without CI shown), providing better evidence of PRS signal. While PGS004478 has a larger stated training sample and larger validation N, those are weak tie-breakers here and it also has “covariates: Unknown,” whereas PGS002763 discloses standard demographic/PC covariates, improving comparability and interpretability.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to gout (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). PGS001789 provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out / pgs_only_r2=0.0312), which is directly usable for PRS strength comparison and is below the gout heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0525), making it plausible. In contrast, PGS004047 reports only full-model metrics (AUROC and R²) with no PGS-only AUC/R², so its performance evidence is less comparable for standalone PRS ranking despite having effect sizes; additionally, its development is single-cohort (UKB) with smaller stated training n=6,704, whereas PGS001789 comes from a broad multi-biobank global framework with multi-ancestry GWAS inputs and large validation (n=359,345), supporting robustness. Overall, PGS001789 has stronger directly comparable PRS-only performance evidence plus broader cohort/ancestry context than PGS004047.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication, have the same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the small full-model AUROC difference (0.639 for PGS005270 vs 0.630 for PGS005271) is not a reliable differentiator. Under the domain guidance, structural signals and PRS-specific effect sizes matter more here: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.55, β≈0.44), consistent with meaningful PRS discrimination, whereas PGS005270 is a sparse P+T score with 55 variants and a near-null effect size (OR≈1.04, β≈0.04), suggesting weak PRS signal despite slightly higher full-model AUROC. Therefore PGS005271 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

PGS002763 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is directly “Hip osteoarthritis,” whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a treatment/proxy endpoint that can reflect access/surgical decision and disease severity rather than hip OA status. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS002728’s full-model AUROC=0.66 (with age/sex covariates) is not a comparable PRS metric and shouldn’t outweigh phenotype mismatch. Structurally, PGS002763 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.05M variants and shows a moderate per-SD OR=1.38, while PGS002728 is a sparse 44-variant GWS score with no effect-size evidence shown. Both are EUR-only evaluation; PGS002763 also has a larger validation sample (39,444 vs 14,926), which mildly supports it but is secondary to the endpoint and structural advantages.

PGS005097 is the better-supported heart failure PRS on endpoint/study-design grounds: it comes from a heart-failure–focused Nat Genet architecture study with a clearly stated diagnosis endpoint (“Prevalent heart failure”) and basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), and it uses a cross-ancestry shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with broader GWAS ancestry input and some non-EUR evaluation context noted. PGS001790, while it reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.006981, below the heritability ceiling) and has much larger EUR validation (n=358,905), is from a known portability/framework-style paper (“Global Biobank analyses…”) and uses a heavier covariate set; its higher full-model AUROC (0.75 vs 0.72) is not PRS-only and is therefore discounted. Given the framework-penalty and stronger disease-focused archetype for PGS005097, it wins despite lacking explicit PRS-only AUC/R2.

PGS005097 is the better-supported heart failure PRS because its endpoint is a direct heart failure diagnosis (trait_efo=heart failure; phenotyping_reported=Prevalent heart failure) and it comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort architecture study with many development cohorts (BBJ, BioMe, CKB, FinnGen, GBMI, HERMES, MVP, etc.), which is a strong transportability signal versus the single-cohort MVP development in PGS005083. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the slightly higher full-model C-index/AUROC in PGS005083 (0.754 vs 0.72) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage, especially given different covariate sets (PGS005083 uses 20 PCs vs 5 PCs). While PGS005083 does report an OR per SD (~1.46), it is tied to a narrower PheCode CHF NOS endpoint and a portability/method-comparison study archetype, whereas PGS005097 has cleaner trait alignment to generic heart failure and broader multi-ancestry GWAS composition with a sizable validation (n=40,989).

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = Hodgkin’s disease/lymphoma), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI), same training n=736, same validation n=775, and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is only a weak within-family signal. Within this matched context, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger performance/effect evidence than PGS000638: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62). With endpoint and design otherwise identical, these aligned advantages make PGS000639 better supported.

PGS001790 is the better-supported heart failure PRS because it provides a clean PRS-comparable performance metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.006981) on an exactly aligned endpoint (Heart failure; EFO heart failure) with basic covariates, and it comes from a broad multi-biobank development context with large EUR evaluation (n=358,905). PGS005083 has a reasonably aligned but narrower phecode endpoint (CHF NOS) and reports only full-model discrimination (C-index ~0.754) without any PRS-only AUC/R2; its OR=1.455 is supportive but below the strong-evidence threshold (≈1.5) and the validation sample is much smaller (n=31,804). With full-model AUC/C-index not being PRS-comparable, PGS001790’s explicit PRS-only R2 and stronger external-validation context outweigh PGS005083’s effect-size-only evidence.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), come from the same publication, have identical EUR-only ancestry context, identical training size (n=736), validation size (n=775), and the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so ranking hinges on the available full-model/effect-size evidence. PGS000638 shows consistently stronger reported performance in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.601 vs 0.574; Nagelkerke R² 0.0193 vs 0.013; OR per SD 1.377 vs 1.30; β 0.32 vs 0.262), while PGS000637’s only edge is being genome-wide (PRS-CS, 1,047,511 variants) and a trivially higher top-1% OR (1.67 vs 1.62) with very wide CIs. Given same endpoint and covariates, the better observed discrimination/effect-size package favors PGS000638, though confidence is moderated because metrics are full-model (not PRS-only) and differences are modest.

Both candidates are near-clones for the hyperthyroidism target: same endpoint fidelity (Graves’ disease; phenotyping_reported graves’ disease), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC reported, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). With design/metadata essentially tied, PGS005265 has slightly stronger visible performance signals: marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and stronger effect sizes (OR 1.63 vs 1.54; β 0.486 vs 0.434). The differences are small, so confidence is low.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), come from the same publication, use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and have identical EUR-only training/evaluation context and sample sizes (training n=736; validation n=775), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so full-model AUROC is only a secondary within-family signal. Within this near-clone setting, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger empirical performance/effect evidence than PGS000637: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.574), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.013), and a stronger per-SD OR (1.476 vs 1.3). Given identical endpoint fidelity and covariate cleanliness, these stronger discrimination/effect-size signals make PGS000639 better supported despite PGS000637’s more complex method and much larger variant count.

PGS005265 is better supported for the target trait (hyperthyroidism) because its endpoint is Graves’ disease, which is a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused multi-biobank study with broad external evaluation context (many contributing cohorts; eval MAE 100%; validation n=94,651) and a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.63), suggesting meaningful PRS signal. PGS001043 has an exact-label match (hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) and clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.6323, R2=0.0216; below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants, UKB-only development), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable in external generalization than disease-focused multi-cohort scores. Given the framework penalty and the stronger disease-focused evidence/effect size for PGS005265 despite lacking PRS-only AUROC/R2, PGS005265 is the stronger choice overall.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=19,883), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiators are structural/performance: PGS002031 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (6,713 vs 654) and shows slightly higher partial correlation in the selected European validation record (0.1355 vs 0.1307). Given identical study context, the higher-coverage shrinkage model with marginally better PRS-comparable metric is better supported than the sparser penalized-regression sibling (PGS001823).

PGS000114 is the better match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to the umbrella JIA endpoint, whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular JIA subtype (endpoint mismatch for a generic JIA target). Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have similar basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC is shown and is not decisive). Although PGS000325 shows a higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.738) and larger validation N, those are weak differentiators given subtype mismatch and non-PRS-only metrics; PGS000114 also has a slightly stronger OR per SD (2.085 vs 1.93).

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet paper with identical endpoint fidelity (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported both hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), identical covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), identical EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same training cohorts, and same validation sample size (n=343,182). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC/R² are only weakly informative; however, within this matched design PGS004911 shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect evidence than PGS004910 (full-model AUROC 0.80 vs 0.73; R² 0.048 vs 0.031; HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5). Additionally, PGS004911 is the MTAG-enhanced variant, which is mildly preferred per the provided domain guidance when all else is equal.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are hypothyroidism). However, PGS005218’s only discrimination evidence is a full-model AUROC=0.859 while using heavy, near-outcome thyroid biomarkers as covariates (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making that AUROC largely non-comparable to standalone PRS performance and not a valid substitute for PGS-only metrics. PGS002766, despite smaller validation (n=39,444) and lacking AUC/R2, provides a PRS-specific effect size (OR per SD=1.47, 95% CI 1.43–1.52) under basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), which is cleaner evidence of genetic score signal for hypothyroidism than a biomarker-inflated full-model AUROC. Net: PGS002766 is better-supported as a PRS for hypothyroidism on the visible fields.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait juvenile idiopathic arthritis because its endpoint fidelity is an exact match at all key fields (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all JIA), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a different EFO and phenotyping_reported, making it less directly aligned to the umbrella target. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), have the same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.738 vs 0.76) are not decisive. With metrics largely non-comparable, the exact endpoint match plus stronger per-SD effect size evidence in PGS000114 (OR 2.085 vs 1.51) outweighs PGS000326’s larger validation N and slightly higher full-model AUROC.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R², so the full-model AUROC values (0.80 for PGS004911 vs 0.821 for PGS000739) are not decisive or directly comparable. PGS004911 is better-supported as a standalone PRS because it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (374,114 vs 27), reports PRS-linked effect sizes (HR 2.34; OR per SD 1.33; plus high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9), and its evaluation model uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), reducing risk of covariate-driven inflation. In contrast, PGS000739’s reported performance is tied to a much heavier clinical package (multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status), making its AUROC less informative about the PRS itself. Validation size is larger for PGS004911 as well (343,182 vs 184,511), but this is secondary to the cleaner covariate context and stronger PRS construction.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because it is from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) with a much larger variant set (107 vs 19) and a substantially stronger PRS effect size signal (OR per SD 1.5 vs PGS000076 HR 1.16), suggesting meaningfully higher standalone genetic discrimination. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and only report full-model AUROC (0.74 vs 0.722), which is not directly comparable as PRS evidence; covariate sets are similarly epidemiologic (age/sex/PCs plus BMI/smoking/hypertension), so the small AUROC difference is weak. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, with PGS000076 mapping to renal cell carcinoma (dominant kidney cancer subtype) and incident kidney cancer, but its cross-cancer evaluation framing and weaker effect size make it less compelling than the disease-focused, higher-signal PGS004908.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a valid PRS discriminator; moreover PGS000739’s higher AUROC (0.821 vs 0.73) is paired with much heavier covariates including multiple clinical risk factors and rare-variant carrier status, making its performance more likely covariate-driven and less comparable to a standalone PRS. PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that leakage concern, and provides supportive PRS signal via effect sizes (e.g., HR 1.97, OR high vs median tertile 5.5) alongside a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with far broader variant coverage (374,190 vs 27). Validation is also larger for PGS004910 (343,182 vs 184,511) though this is a weak tie-break. Overall, PGS004910 is better-supported as a cleaner PRS for HCM, while PGS000739 looks more like a clinically augmented risk model.

PGS005218 is better supported overall: it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with much broader multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.), far larger training (n=1,146,562) and evaluation (n=441,692) than PGS004935 (UKB-only training; eval n=8,417). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported full-model AUROCs are not directly comparable PRS metrics; moreover PGS005218’s very high AUROC (0.859) is paired with explicit thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) in covariates, making that AUROC likely covariate-inflated and not strong PRS evidence. However, PGS004935 is a portability/framework-style UKB-derived sparse SnpNet score with limited supporting metadata (covariates unknown) and only modest full-model AUROC (0.7) plus an OR=1.5; given the framework penalty and weaker study support, PGS005218’s stronger endpoint specificity (incident hypothyroidism) and substantially stronger multi-cohort evidence package outweigh its covariate-heavy performance reporting.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to hypothyroidism (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC in PGS004935 (0.70) is not a comparable PRS metric. With metrics largely non-informative, structural signals dominate: PGS002766 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with far broader variant coverage (1,092,122 vs 6,127 for PGS004935), which is generally better suited for polygenic disease prediction than a sparse model. Effect sizes are similar (OR 1.47 vs 1.50), and both are EUR-only UKB-based; PGS002766 also discloses basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/technical), whereas PGS004935 has unknown covariates, lowering interpretability. Overall, PGS002766 is better-supported on method/coverage and covariate transparency given the lack of PRS-only performance metrics in both.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported kidney cancer; trait_efo renal cell carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident kidney cancer), use the same covariates, same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same variant count (19), and show essentially identical full-model discrimination and HR (PGS000076 AUROC 0.722, HR 1.16 vs PGS000787 AUROC 0.722, HR 1.15). However, PGS000787 is explicitly a derivative of PGS000076 (“19 variants from Graff et al (PGS000076) with inverse variant weights”), offering no independent training/endpoint advantage and potentially introducing a sign/weighting concern without any compensating PRS-only metric. PGS000076 is the original score from the cross-cancer evaluation paper and has broader supporting metadata (multiple performance records vs 1), so it is better-supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_efo is late-onset Alzheimer’s disease; phenotyping_reported is late-onset AD). However, PGS000054 has cleaner and more interpretable PRS evidence: it reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93), whereas PGS000334 provides only an R²=0.191 that appears to be a generic/full-model variance-explained metric (not explicitly PRS-only) with unknown covariates, making it less comparable and potentially inflated. PGS000054 also has explicitly basic covariates (age, sex) and a broad multi-cohort disease-focused development context, while PGS000334’s development is limited to IGAP/UKB and lacks covariate transparency. Validation sample sizes are similar (3,324 vs 3,810), so they don’t break the tie; overall the stronger, cleaner PRS signal favors PGS000054.

PGS004908 is better supported for the target “kidney cancer” because it is a disease-focused, kidney-cancer GWAS meta-analysis score with strong PRS signal (OR per SD 1.5 [1.43–1.58]) and a substantially richer variant set (107 GWAS-significant SNPs) than PGS000787 (19 variants, explicitly derived from another score with inverse weights). PGS002246 is better supported for the target melanoma endpoint because its phenotyping is explicitly aligned to a clean clinical outcome (“Incident invasive melanoma”) with only basic covariates (age, sex), making the reported discrimination less likely to be covariate-inflated. Both are EUR-only, similar GWAS-hit methods and variant counts, and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2; given that, the cleaner endpoint/covariate design in PGS002246 outweighs PGS000743’s covariate-heavy full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (melanoma), identical endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same publication and validation sample size (n=4,765), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model metrics, which are not strong PRS-comparable differentiators). Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, the variant-count advantage is the more meaningful tie-break, favoring PGS002247.

PGS002247 is better supported for the target melanoma endpoint because its phenotyping is explicitly aligned to a clean clinical outcome (“Incident invasive melanoma”) with only basic covariates (age, sex), making the reported discrimination less likely to be covariate-inflated. In contrast, PGS000743 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.74) but uses an extensive traditional risk-factor bundle including family history and other strong non-genetic predictors, so its higher AUROC is not interpretable as stronger PRS performance and is heavily discounted without PGS-only/incremental metrics. Both are EUR-only GWAS/EVAL and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the cleaner endpoint/covariate design and larger variant set (68 vs 45) favor PGS002247.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful to multiple myeloma (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and are near-identical structurally (GWAS-significant variants, 23 variants, EUR-only GWAS and EUR-only evaluation). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC difference (0.69 in PGS002306 vs 0.644 in PGS002281) is not a clean PRS-comparable advantage, especially with PGS002306 having unknown covariates. PGS002281 provides clearer evaluation context (covariates explicitly listed: age, sex, geographic region) and includes an additional PRS-relevant effect-size signal (OR highest vs lowest quintiles = 3.18 [2.34–4.33]) plus a much larger validation sample (n=2,395 vs n=290), making its evidence package better supported overall than PGS002306.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma) and both are EUR-only with only basic covariates, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only weakly comparable). Given that, PGS002281 has stronger visible validation evidence: higher full-model AUROC (0.644 vs 0.577) and a stronger stratification OR (highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18 vs top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1 for PGS000653). PGS000653 has a listed training sample size and per-SD effect size, but it comes from a repository-style cross-cancer framework paper and its performance signals are weaker overall. Both candidates target the same endpoint (age-related macular degeneration) with identical phenotyping_reported and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not directly comparable as a standalone PRS metric). Although PGS004607 has a GWAS ancestry mismatch (AFR GWAS, EUR eval), its endpoint fidelity and stronger structural PRS properties outweigh PGS004952’s sparse 52-SNP GWS score and non-comparable full-model AUROC.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distributions, same validation size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS002306 (0.69) is not a clean PRS advantage. Overall, PGS000653 is better-supported and more interpretable on the visible metadata.

Both candidates align to the target trait (AMD) at trait_reported/trait_efo and use only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS004952 adds survey membership but no clear leakage). Overall, PGS004606 is better supported as a standalone PRS for macular degeneration than the sparse 52-SNP GWS score in PGS004952 whose apparent AUROC advantage is full-model and potentially non-comparable.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (ICD10 J33 nasal polyp), same publication, same EUR-only dev/eval, same training cohort (UKB), same training N (174,489), same validation N (56,192), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (no pgs_only_auc/r2). Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/EFO (benign nodular goiter), same phenotyping string, same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry distribution (MAE 100%), same validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 with covariates unknown—so full-model AUROC is only a weak differentiator. Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported identical aside from a typo), come from the same publication family, have the same evaluation ancestry mix and the same validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a clean PRS-comparable metric). PGS000082 better matches the generic target of “ovarian neoplasm” via a direct disease endpoint (“Incident ovarian cancer”), whereas PGS003394 is packaged as horizon-specific prediction (“10-year ovarian cancer risks”), which is a known negative signal for standalone PRS comparability. PGS001855 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² and only provides partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625), which is less directly comparable as a discrimination metric. Although PGS001855 has more variants (1505 vs 179) and larger training N, the absence of PRS-only metrics makes its empirical support weaker here, so PGS001306 wins on cleaner, directly interpretable PRS performance evidence.

PGS000014 is better supported as a standalone T2D PRS: it reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only Nagelkerke R2=0.029 after basic covariate adjustment) and comes from a disease-focused multi-cohort development context (DIAGRAM/EPIC/GERA/UKB) with large validation (n=288,978) and broad multi-ancestry evaluation. In contrast, PGS003103 is from the ExPRSweb framework/repository archetype (a known weaker study type for per-disease optimization), provides only full-model time-to-event discrimination (C-index=0.759) plus HR without any PRS-only AUC/R2, and uses an incident T2D endpoint that is less directly aligned to generic T2D status than PGS000014’s direct T2D phenotyping. The full-model C-index advantage for PGS003103 is not comparable to PRS-only performance, so PGS000014 has the stronger visible evidence package.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (squamous cell carcinoma), same publication, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (8,029), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same validation N (8,473). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the small full-model AUROC difference (PGS000463 0.593 vs PGS000465 0.589) is not a strong differentiator. With metrics essentially tied, PGS000465 gets a slight edge from stronger effect-size evidence (top 1% vs rest OR 4.54 vs 3.74; per-SD OR 1.457 vs 1.448) and a modestly higher pseudo-R² (0.0282 vs 0.0268), while remaining equally endpoint-faithful and comparably adjusted.

PGS001864 is the better-supported match to the target trait urolithiasis on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is exactly urolithiasis and phenotyping_reported is a direct diagnosis-style “Urinary calculus,” whereas PGS001250 is explicitly a time-to-event phenotype (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”) and maps to narrower EFOs (nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis), which is a mild mismatch for a generic urolithiasis target. Although PGS001250 has clean PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.5668; PGS R2 0.00592) and a larger validation sample, it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”), which is a generalizability warning signal; PGS001864 is also a framework/portability paper but uses a denser penalized regression score (5599 variants vs 341) and includes broader multi-ancestry evaluation. Confidence is low because both candidates are UKB framework-style scores and PGS001864 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2, making the performance comparison incomplete.

PGS001795 is the better-supported choice for the target trait “uterine cancer” because its endpoint matches the umbrella trait directly (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: “Uterine cancer”, trait_efo: uterine carcinoma) and it reports a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R² = 0.001948), which is interpretable against the provided low heritability ceiling. In contrast, PGS003381 targets the dominant subtype (endometrial carcinoma) rather than the umbrella uterine cancer label and provides only full-model AUROC/R² (0.761/0.11) without any PGS-only metric, making its apparent performance likely covariate-influenced and not directly comparable for PRS quality. Both use only basic demographic/PC covariates and EUR evaluation, so the key differentiators are endpoint fidelity and availability of PRS-only performance evidence, favoring PGS001795.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported Bladder cancer; trait_efo urinary bladder carcinoma; phenotyping_reported Cancer of bladder), use the same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (so the very similar full-model AUROC ~0.57 is not a strong differentiator). PGS000613 is better supported structurally and empirically: it has a larger training sample (12,992 vs 7,469), slightly more variants (15 vs 13) with a more general P+T construction rather than a strict GWAS-hits set, and a clearly stronger risk stratification metric (OR top 1% vs rest 2.91 [1.99–4.24] vs 1.47 [0.779–2.77], where the latter is weak/uncertain). Given near-identical endpoint/covariate context, these differences favor PGS000613.

PGS003381 is better supported for the target “uterine cancer” because its endpoint is a clinically dominant and closely aligned subtype (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported: uterine endometrial carcinoma; trait_efo: endometrial carcinoma), and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (lassosum) with very large variant coverage (529,365) and a much larger European validation sample (n=144,479). PGS000541 matches the umbrella label exactly (malignant neoplasm of uterus; trait_efo: uterine cancer) but appears to be a sparse GWAS-hits score (18 variants) from a repository/framework-style paper with weaker reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.576 vs 0.761) and smaller validation (n=6,987). Neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the decision relies on endpoint fidelity plus structural/model strength and validation context, favoring PGS003381 despite the subtype vs umbrella-label difference.

PGS002308 is from a disease-focused trans-ancestry T2D PRS development/validation study and uses PRS-CSx with broader GWAS ancestry input (AFR/EAS/EUR) and very broad multi-ancestry evaluation, which is supportive for transportability to diverse populations. It also reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.96), comparable in magnitude to PGS003103’s HR=1.89. By contrast, PGS003103 comes from the ExPRSweb framework/repository paper (a known pan-trait/framework archetype) and uses EUR-only GWAS/DEV, with an incident time-to-event endpoint (“Incident type 2 diabetes”) that is a mild endpoint mismatch versus the generic target disease risk. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R², and the full-model C-index/AUROC values (0.759 vs 0.793) are not PRS-comparable and use different covariate setups, so they should not drive selection; thus the stronger study archetype + trans-ancestry design favors PGS002308.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait urolithiasis because its endpoint is a direct disease diagnosis match (trait_efo=urolithiasis; phenotyping_reported="Urinary calculus") and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (731,196), plus it is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS), supporting portability beyond EUR. PGS001250 does provide clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.5668; PGS-only R2=0.00592) but it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework ("across 813 traits"; snpnet with only 341 variants) and uses a time-to-event phenotype (TTE calculus of kidney and ureter), which is a less faithful match to the generic urolithiasis endpoint and a weaker archetype for external generalization. Overall, the structural and endpoint-fidelity advantages of PGS002075 outweigh PGS001250’s modest PRS-only metric reporting.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported, same GWAS-hits method with 13 variants, same EUR-only ancestry, same basic covariates, same publication/date, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—only full-model AUROC/R2 which are not PRS-comparable). The only substantive differences are small full-model metric shifts (PGS000610 AUROC 0.572 vs 0.567) that are likely noise, and effect-size/stratification evidence plus sample context: PGS000611 has a much stronger top-1% vs rest OR (2.66 vs 1.47) and larger training/validation sample sizes (12,992/13,530 vs 7,469/7,622). Given the lack of PRS-only metrics, the stronger risk stratification signal and broader evaluation support slightly favor PGS000611, but the decision is low-confidence because the records are otherwise extremely similar and the AUROC difference points the other way.

PGS001536 is endpoint-aligned to vitiligo (phenotyping_reported: "TTE vitiligo"; trait_reported explicitly vitiligo time-to-event) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates and a heritability-sane R2 well below the vitiligo h2_obs ceiling (~0.17). In contrast, PGS000760 has a major phenotype mismatch: phenotyping_reported is "anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients" (treatment-induced thyroid toxicity, not vitiligo), and it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only an HR=1.41 and a meta-analysis p-value), making it much less supported for the target trait despite the vitiligo label fields.

PGS001536 is the better-supported vitiligo PRS on the visible fields: it has coherent phenotype alignment (trait_reported vitiligo time-to-event; phenotyping_reported explicitly “TTE vitiligo”) and reports clean PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates only and a large UKB training/validation context. Its PRS-only R2 is also plausibly below the vitiligo heritability ceiling given in the domain knowledge. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/metadata mismatch (phenotyping_reported = “Red hair” despite trait_reported vitiligo), lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, and only provides a pseudo R2/full-model-style metric with unknown covariates, making its evidence package internally inconsistent and less reliable for vitiligo risk prediction.

PGS001795 is the better-supported uterine cancer PRS on the visible fields because it provides a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) with basic covariates and a very large European evaluation sample (n=170,276), and its endpoint fields are directly aligned (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: uterine cancer; trait_efo: uterine carcinoma). The PRS-only R2 is also below the provided uterine-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005; liability≈0.0116), making it at least sanity-consistent. PGS000541 has reasonable endpoint alignment (malignant neoplasm of uterus) and reports effect sizes (OR per SD 1.31; top 1% vs rest OR 2.12), but it lacks any PRS-only AUC/R2 and its reported AUROC (0.576) is full-model, with a much smaller validation sample (n=6,987) and a sparse 18-variant GWAS-hits construction that is structurally less likely to capture polygenic signal than the genome-wide PRS-CS-auto score in PGS001795. Overall, PGS001795 has stronger directly comparable PRS evidence and broader evaluation support, while PGS000541’s evidence is less PRS-isolated and more limited.

PGS000738 is better supported for the target trait vitiligo because its publication context is vitiligo-focused and its reported evaluation appears to be on a vitiligo-relevant setting (trait_reported/trait_efo both vitiligo) with a direct PRS performance proxy reported (pseudo R²=0.0386) in a larger validation sample (n=4,702). In contrast, PGS000760 has a major endpoint-fidelity mismatch in phenotyping_reported (anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients), which is treatment-induced and thyroid-related rather than vitiligo disease status; its only reported effect size is an HR=1.41 in that therapy-specific context and it lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R². Despite PGS000760’s larger training sample (n=408,959) and basic covariates (5 PCs), the phenotype mismatch dominates, making PGS000738 the more appropriate vitiligo PRS candidate on the visible fields.
